title: Silko, βασιλίσκος of the Nobades, in the temple of Mandulis at Talmis — a Greek victory inscription in a Roman temple
language_note: Koine Greek, cut on the pronaos wall of the Roman-period temple of Mandulis at Talmis. The Greek is late and irregular -- ἀναχωρήθην and ἐγεγονέμην are not classical forms -- and that is part of what the record carries: this is a Nubian king's chancery writing the empire's language, not the empire writing about him.
date: 5th century CE (PHI: '5th c. AD?'). The question mark is the edition's own and is kept: Silko's date rests on his relation to the Blemmyes-Nobades conflict and is not fixed by the stone.
findspot: Pronaos wall of the temple of Mandulis, Talmis (Kalabsha), Lower Nubia — inside the Dodecaschoenus, the strip the Roman empire had held and withdrawn from under Diocletian.
original_text_excerpt: [Withdrawn from the public history under RULINGS 98 and 102: this Greek was copied from PHI Greek Inscriptions, whose terms restrict use to personal study. The record's Greek since 2026-09-23 is OGIS 201.]
original_text_note: Verbatim Koine Greek, lines 1-3, COPIED BY HAND from PHI Greek Inscriptions OGIS 201 (epigraphy.packhum.org/text/219058) on 2026-08-31. Two editorial acts, declared: PHI's marginal line numbers are omitted, and the line-break hyphen in ἐπο-λέμησα is closed up. Nothing else is altered. FINDING 48 is why this note says COPIED BY HAND, and this record is its second measurement: an automated fetch of this same page was compared against the hand copy over 431 characters and differed in one, substituting U+0027 for U+2019 in μετ’ αὐτῶν -- the same substitution measured on the Adulis page, so the normalisation is systematic and not incidental.
reference_translation: I, Silko, king of the Noubades and all the Ethiopians, came twice to Talmis and Taphis, I warred with the Blemmys and the God gave me the victory.
translation_source: Helmut Satzinger, 'The Inscription of Silko, King of the Noubades', at homepage.univie.ac.at/helmut.satzinger/Wurzelverzeichnis/Silko_Inscription.html. READ THIS FIELD WITH THE NOTE BELOW: it is a named Egyptologist's own rendering on a personal university page, it cites no published edition, and the page carries no bibliography. It is the weakest translation provenance in this corpus and it is named rather than dressed up.
reference_translation_note:
THREE THINGS A READER HAS TO KNOW, and none of them is visible from the text alone.

1. THE TWO EDITIONS DISAGREE ABOUT WHERE THE SENTENCE ENDS. PHI punctuates ἦλθον εἰς Τάλμιν καὶ Τάφιν. ἅπαξ δύο ἐπολέμησα -- 'I came to Talmis and Taphis. Twice I warred'. Satzinger reads ἦλθον εἰς Τάλμιν καὶ Τάφιν ἅπαξ δύο as one clause -- 'came twice to Talmis and Taphis'. Same characters, different sentence boundary, different meaning, and the English here follows a reading the Greek here does not print. The corpus pairs them anyway and says so, because a record that quietly pairs a source chunk with an English translating a different segmentation is worse than one that declares it. The alternative was to cut the excerpt until two editions agreed, which would have meant choosing the passage by the convenience of the alignment rather than by what the text says.

2. βασιλίσκος IS RENDERED 'king'. The diminutive is the reason this record is in the corpus: it is the Greco-Roman word for a client king on the empire's edge, and an African ruler applied it to himself, in Greek, in a Roman temple. The English loses it.

3. THE TRANSLATION IS NOT TEXT. Satzinger's page presents both the Greek and the English as JPEG images; the only text on it is a quotation from Wikipedia about Nobatia. This English was typed out by the curator from a picture. See the record's own notes.
citation_original: PHI Greek Inscriptions, OGIS 201 = Kalabschah 204; Lefebvre 628; Prose sur pierre 67; SB 5.8536; SEG 18.722.
notes:
F4, record 32, and Sub-Saharan Africa's third record carrying retrieval-eligible source-language text. WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT ROME: Silko calls himself βασιλίσκος -- the Greco-Roman diminutive used of client kings on the empire's frontier -- writes in Greek on the wall of a temple the Roman empire built, in the Dodecaschoenus it had abandoned under Diocletian, and credits ὁ θεός with his victory. The influence is in the vocabulary, the language, the building and the god, and in nothing the Romans did.

A FOURTH STATE THE TIER CANNOT SEE, recorded here because it was found on this record. Ruling 57 defines verbatim_machine_english by whether a curator can REACH an English translation. This one is reachable -- free, open, on the web, a person reads it in a second -- and it is not CAPTURABLE by anything except a human retyping it, because it is pixels. Reachable and capturable are two different properties, the tier only asks about the first, and the record needs the second. This record is verbatim_with_provenance and that is correct; what the tier could not have told anyone is that its English cost a person typing from a photograph.

AND THE CAPTURE WAS CHECKED, which had never happened here before. The typed English diverged from the image in five places -- two dropped definite articles, two altered stops, and 'my upper part' becoming 'the upper part' with a doubled preposition. FINDING 48 says nothing between the page and the record may be a model. It does not say nothing may compare them afterwards, and the difference is the whole of FINDING 50.

NOT gloss-capable. Satzinger prints a bare '(?)' against Telelis at line 16, which is outside this excerpt and is a hedge about a place-name reading rather than a published alternative reading with a statement of uncertainty. F4's two gloss-capable records are still owed.
